data.title: Air pollution in India: Does health insurance cover pollution-related illnesses? What policyholders should know
data.description:
New Delhi, Nov. 7 -- With Diwali celebrations bringing families together, health protection deserves as much attention as festive shopping and financial planning. For people living in cities that regularly experience poor air quality, respiratory illnesses such as asthma, bronchitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and respiratory infections can be a particular concern, especially as pollution levels rise during the winter months.

While health insurance can help cover the financial burden of hospitalisation due to respiratory complications, policyholders should not assume that every pollution-related medical expense will be reimbursed.

Shrish Mahuli, Chief Business Officer at SBI General Insurance, said claims arising from respiratory conditions are assessed based on the nature of the illness, the insured person's medical history and the applicable policy provisions. Policyholders should check waiting periods, exclusions and other conditions to understand the extent of their coverage.

Generally, health insurance policies cover medically necessary hospitalisation for respiratory conditions such as asthma, bronchitis, COPD and respiratory infections, subject to policy terms and conditions.

However, coverage is primarily for eligible hospitalisation expenses and does not necessarily extend to routine outpatient treatment. Doctor consultations, inhalers, over-the-counter medicines and nebulisers used at home are generally not covered unless the policy offers outpatient department (OPD) benefits.

Vineet Gupta, Head of Product Development at ManipalCigna Health Insurance, said coverage is determined by the medical condition and the need for hospitalisation rather than whether pollution caused or aggravated the illness.

Ajay Shah, MD and CEO of Care Health Insurance, said eligible in-patient hospitalisation expenses can include room rent, ICU charges, doctors' fees, medicines, diagnostic tests, ambulance services and pre- and post-hospitalisation expenses, subject to the policy's limits.

This is particularly important for individuals who already have asthma, COPD or other respiratory conditions.

If air pollution aggravates an existing condition, the claim may be treated as a claim relating to a pre-existing disease. In such cases, the policyholder must have completed the applicable waiting period for the treatment expenses to become eligible.

Gupta said most health insurance policies have a PED waiting period of 36 months, although the duration varies across products. Some insurers allow customers to reduce this period by paying an additional premium. Certain policies may also offer coverage for declared and accepted pre-existing conditions from day one.

Policyholders should disclose existing respiratory conditions, previous diagnoses and regular medication at the time of purchasing health insurance. Non-disclosure can create complications when filing claims.

Severe respiratory complications can sometimes require emergency hospitalisation, oxygen support or intensive care. Health insurance can provide financial protection against these expenses when the treatment meets the policy's conditions.

Gupta said hospitalisation involving oxygen support and ICU treatment is covered under standard health insurance policies when medically necessary. However, the hospitalisation must meet the minimum continuous hospital stay requirement specified in the policy.

Mahuli said the admissibility of such claims depends on medical necessity, the treating doctor's recommendations and the applicable policy provisions. Policyholders should also check ICU coverage, room rent limits and the sum insured to understand their financial protection.

With respiratory illnesses potentially affecting multiple family members, choosing an adequate sum insured becomes important.

Shah said families living in cities with persistently poor air quality should consider policies with automatic restoration benefits. These allow the sum insured to be replenished after it is exhausted, subject to policy conditions, helping cover subsequent hospitalisations.

A super top-up policy can also increase the overall health cover at a relatively lower premium. However, consumers should check its deductible and other conditions before buying one.

A policy with a high sum insured may still leave policyholders with substantial out-of-pocket expenses if it has restrictive conditions. Room rent caps, ICU limits, co-payment clauses and disease-specific sub-limits can reduce the amount an insurer pays towards a hospital bill.

Shah recommends checking for policies without room rent or ICU capping and disease-wise sub-limits. Such restrictions can affect the final claim settlement and, in some cases, result in proportionate deductions.

Mahuli also advises consumers to examine ambulance cover and pre- and post-hospitalisation benefits when comparing policies.

Not every pollution-related health problem requires hospitalisation. Many respiratory conditions are managed through regular doctor consultations, diagnostic tests, lung-function assessments and medication.

Standard health insurance policies generally do not cover these routine expenses unless they include OPD benefits.

Gupta recommends checking whether a policy offers OPD or chronic-care add-ons that can help meet expenses such as consultations, diagnostics and inhalers. A wide cashless hospital network and e-consultation facilities can also be useful.

Shah highlighted the importance of understanding which family members are most vulnerable to respiratory illnesses.

According to Care Health Insurance's claims data, children aged 0-12 accounted for 40% of its respiratory hospitalisation claims in FY26, while senior citizens aged 60 and above accounted for 17%. Together, these age groups contributed 58% of such claims during the year.

Ultimately, consumers should look beyond the headline sum insured when buying health insurance. Waiting periods, exclusions, hospitalisation benefits, restoration features and coverage for routine medical expenses all determine how useful a policy can be when a family member needs treatment.

For families living in cities with poor air quality, reviewing these details before the winter pollution season sets in can help avoid unpleasant surprises at the time of a claim.

data.title: Trending stocks this week as Wall Street ends sharply lower
data.description:
The U.S. stock market was marked this week by a historical midterm election result as Democrats took control of House and Senate.

In the immediate aftermath of the midterms, concerns about elevated AI valuations and heavy technology-sector spending triggered a sharp sell-off, particularly in semiconductor stocks.

Technology stocks rebounded on the last day of trade, but not enough to erase the week's losses. The major indices still ended the week in red. The S&P 500 was down around 3%, Nasdaq Composite declined 4% and Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 1.7%.

In economy-related news, the October U.S. jobs report showed stronger-than-expected job growth, raising expectations of a Fed rate hike in December, adding another source of uncertainty for equities.

Amid a turbulent week for Wall Street, here were some of the stocks that caught the attention of investors:

Tesla and SpaceX dropped soon after the elections as Elon Musk's $500M bet on Republican campaigns proved unsuccessful. Both stocks rebounded somewhat on Friday but still ended in the red. Tesla was down 11.3% and SpaceX declined 2%. Musk also said on Friday that Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production in 2027 because of underwhelming sales.

AI and semiconductor stocks tumbled on Thursday as investors pulled back from technology stocks amid concerns over the outlook for data center spending following the U.S. midterm elections. The selloff came a day after Democrats secured a majority in Congress. Chipmakers bore the brunt of the declines. Advanced Micro Devices fell 17%, Intel lost 10.3%, Broadcom declined 10.4%, Nvidia dropped 9.2%, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing fell 10.7%.

Marvell announced a definitive agreement to acquire Lumentum , an optical components manufacturer, in an all-stock transaction with an implied enterprise value of $115B. Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 shares of Marvell common stock for each Lumentum share they own. The acquisition is intended to strengthen Marvell's position in AI data center connectivity and optical technologies.

AppLovin shares surged more than 31% following its third-quarter earnings announcement. Revenue increased 55% year over year to $2.185B, while net income climbed 72% to $1.44B. The strong results were driven in part by improvements to its AI-powered advertising technology.

Qualcomm's shares fell nearly 10% on Thursday after its smartphone chip revenue tumbled 26% in the fourth quarter as rising memory prices weighed on handset demand. Overall, Qualcomm said it earned an adjusted $2.17 per share in the quarter as revenue fell 7% year-over-year to come in at $10.44B.

Apple reported fiscal fourth-quarter results that topped Wall Street's estimates. For the period ending Sept. 26, Apple said it earned $2.10 per share as revenue rose 12% year-over-year to come in at $114.48B. However, shares slipped as Apple forecast gross margins of 45%–46% for the December quarter, down from 47.9% in the September quarter. Following the report, CEO John Ternus warned that memory-chip prices were rising at an unprecedented rate.

Palantir Technologies shares fell even as the company reported strong third-quarter results and issued an upward revision to its full-year outlook, as investors focused on a slowdown in U.S. commercial bookings. U.S. commercial revenue surged 148% Y/Y to $984M in Q3, while U.S. government revenue jumped 96% to $953M.

Oracle priced a combined $20B stock and bond offering, including a $10B common stock sale at an 11.2% discount to its last closing price, as the company raises fresh capital amid its expanding AI infrastructure investments. The company priced 86.2M shares at $116 a piece, compared with its October 30 closing price of $130.67. The equity offering is expected to generate ~$9.9B in net proceeds. Separately, Oracle () priced $10B of senior notes across five tranches.

AMD reported third-quarter results and guidance that topped Wall Street's forecast. For the period ending Sept. 26, AMD said it earned an adjusted $2.09 per share as revenue rose 45% year-over-year to come in at $13.38B. Data Center revenue rose 97% year-over-year to $8.55B, aided by its MI-series AI accelerators and its Instinct and EPYC processors.

Novo ) raised its outlook for the year once again, driven by continued demand for its Wegovy weight-loss pill, and its older shot Ozempic. The Danish drugmaker now expects sales and operating profit to either decline by 2% or increase by as much as 2% this year at constant exchange rates. The revised forecast compares with its previous outlook, which had projected declines of up to 6%.

data.title: Paraguay's ex-President Peña faces prosecutors after impeachment, house arrest
data.description:
Paraguay’s former President Santiago Peña arrived at the Attorney General’s Office on Saturday to appear before prosecutors, a day after he was impeached and placed under house arrest amid a political and financial crisis triggered by the collapse of digital lender ueno.

Prosecutors said on Friday that charges against Peña were still being determined but could include influence peddling.

His removal brought Vice President Pedro Alliana to power, with the longtime ruling Colorado Party politician sworn in on Friday to complete Peña’s term through August 2028.

Lawmakers who backed Peña’s impeachment accused him of conflicts of interest, manipulating regulatory oversight and participating in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.

Peña, who was a shareholder in ueno’s holding company until March 2025, has denied wrongdoing and said the bank’s problems were a regulatory matter.

The collapse has left millions of customers struggling to access their accounts and prompted protests in Asuncion. The scandal has also swept up senior officials and former ueno executives, while regulators have sought to reassure depositors and contain risks to the wider financial system.

data.title: E20 petrol supplied by PSU oil firms meets prescribed quality standards: Oil Min
data.description:
The government on Saturday defended the 20 per cent ethanol-blended petrol programme, saying tests of 893 samples collected across 27 states and Union Territories, including 56 in Karnataka, found them compliant with prescribed quality standards, as state-run oil companies challenged the Karnataka government's claims of excessive ethanol content in fuel sold at some retail outlets.

The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, in a statement, said Indian Oil Corporation (IOC), Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL) had found ethanol content in all 893 samples within the prescribed 19-21 per cent range under the Bureau of Indian Standards' IS 17021 specification.

The 56 samples tested in Karnataka, covering different locations and all three oil marketing companies (OMCs), recorded ethanol content of 19-20 per cent, averaging 19.30 per cent, the ministry said.

The findings directly contradict a recent press release by Karnataka's Department of Food, Civil Supplies, Consumer Affairs and Legal Metrology, which claimed that petrol samples collected from certain retail outlets in the state contained 26-31 per cent ethanol.

The three OMCs have questioned the sampling and testing procedures adopted in Karnataka's October 2026 exercise, arguing that the reported results cannot be independently validated without compliance with prescribed statutory procedures and disclosure of the technical details of the tests.

The dispute comes at a time when India's nationwide E20 programme, aimed at reducing dependence on imported crude oil and lowering emissions, has come under scrutiny over concerns about vehicle mileage, engine compatibility and the potential cost to consumers.

Under the Motor Spirit and High Speed Diesel (Regulation of Supply, Distribution and Prevention of Malpractices) Order, 2005, read with the Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) 2024, six one-litre samples must be drawn during an inspection. Two are handed to the dealer, two retained by the oil company or department, and two sent to an authorised laboratory.

The OMCs said samples collected during a September exercise were routed through the State Level Coordinator to designated company laboratories, but the subsequent October exercise was reportedly conducted without their representatives.

They said they had not received the corresponding retention samples, complete outlet-wise details or laboratory reports despite seeking them through the State Level Coordinator.

The companies also questioned certificates issued by a third-party laboratory, saying these did not specify the standard test method, dilution procedure or reference material used to determine ethanol content through Gas Chromatography.

Under IS 17021:2018, amended in August 2025, ethanol content must be determined through specified methods, including Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy, water extraction or Gas Chromatography under prescribed ASTM standards.

When Gas Chromatography is used, the standard requires samples to be diluted in a 1:1 ratio with oxygenate-free petrol and results corrected against an E10 certified reference material, the OMCs said.

The companies also flagged density readings of 0.742-0.749 grams per cubic centimetre in samples reportedly containing 26-31% ethanol, compared with 0.752-0.760 grams per cubic centimetre in their own E20 samples. Since ethanol is denser than petrol, a higher ethanol proportion would ordinarily be expected to increase the blend's density, they said.

The OMCs argued that the discrepancies reinforced the need for independent testing using prescribed methods and appropriate reference samples.

The government and OMCs also challenged estimates that E20 fuel could cause annual consumer mileage losses of around Rs 62,000 crore and vehicle repair costs of Rs 39,000 crore, taking the combined estimated burden to approximately Rs 1.01 lakh crore.

Citing studies involving the Inter-Ministerial Committee, Indian Oil, the Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI) and the Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM), the ministry said the mileage impact varied depending on vehicle category and engine calibration.

Vehicles calibrated for E20 could experience mileage reductions of around 1-2 per cent, while certain other vehicles could see declines of 3-6 per cent, according to the Petroleum Ministry's response to concerns over ethanol blending published on August 12, 2025.

The OMCs said applying a blanket assumption of 10% mileage loss across the entire vehicle population was not scientifically established. They also sought supporting vehicle-performance data, materials compatibility studies and documented repair costs for the Rs 39,000 crore repair estimate.

More than 30 crore two-wheelers and 4 crore four-wheelers have been running on E20 fuel for over three years, while more than 6 crore people visit petrol pumps daily, the companies said, arguing that there had been no reported widespread incidence of vehicle breakdowns attributable to fuel quality.

India's ethanol-blending programme, which began with a pilot initiative in 2001, has become a key component of the country's strategy to reduce its dependence on imported crude oil, support agricultural incomes and improve energy security.

According to Petroleum Ministry figures, the programme since the 2014-15 ethanol supply year has generated foreign exchange savings of more than Rs 1.97 lakh crore, substituted approximately 316 lakh metric tonnes of crude oil and reduced carbon dioxide emissions by around 952 lakh metric tonnes.

It has also resulted in payments of more than Rs 1.66 lakh crore to farmers.

During the 2025-26 ethanol supply year, which ended on October 31, 2026, the three public sector OMCs procured 1,089 crore litres of ethanol and blended 1,134 crore litres against petrol sales of approximately 5,673 crore litres, the ministry said.

The companies rejected suggestions that they had a commercial incentive to blend ethanol beyond prescribed levels, saying additional procurement would increase their costs.

The controversy has implications for the credibility of India's ethanol-blending programme, which has been scaled up rapidly as part of efforts to cut oil imports and emissions. While the government cites energy security, environmental and agricultural benefits, questions over fuel quality and vehicle performance could influence consumer confidence and the pace of wider acceptance of E20.

The three OMCs have asked the Karnataka government to share complete sampling documentation, outlet-wise laboratory reports and details of the testing methodology. They have also sought access to counterpart samples for independent testing at an authorised laboratory using the prescribed referee method, in the presence of state government and OMC representatives.

The companies said they were willing to participate in a joint sampling and testing exercise and that any deviation established through the prescribed procedure would be dealt with under applicable guidelines. PTI ANZ
